title: The breath and the Name
hook: the yogis speak of breath practice; Nanak points to the Name within the breath

segments.voice: Yesterday, without the Guru: in the Sidh Gosht, Nanak tells the yogis that no one finds the way alone. Your line was a guide is needed. Who did you thank? Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

A breath went in just now. Nobody asked it to. It will go out in a moment, and another will come, all day, through meetings and traffic and sleep, without a single instruction from you. The yogis who sit across from Guru Nanak in the Sidh Gosht had made a whole discipline out of that quiet traffic: how to hold the breath, slow it, steer it, master it. They bring that up in the conversation, and Nanak doesn't wave it away. He answers. But he points somewhere they might not expect. Today: the breath and the Name.
screen: `A BREATH, WITHOUT INSTRUCTIONS.` → `THE YOGIS: MASTER THE BREATH.` → `NANAK POINTS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Start with what the yogis brought to the mountain. In the dialogue, their path is a path of discipline: postures, earrings, the patched coat, and work with the breath. The breath was something to be trained. Nanak's answers, all through the Sidh Gosht, keep coming back to the Word, the Shabad, held inside. So when talk turns to the breath, the poem doesn't tell anyone to stop breathing that way. Read beside the rest of his answers, the question shifts: not how long the breath is held, but what it carries. That idea runs all through the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani, puts it in a phrase Sikhs still use: saas saas simrahu Gobind. In paraphrase: remember the Lord with every breath, and the worry inside the mind lifts. Notice the shape of that. Not one great breath held for a long time. Every breath. Ordinary ones. The one you took at the red light and the one you'll take in your sleep. The word for this remembering is simran, and some Sikhs do it by letting the Name, Waheguru, ride the breath in and out, quietly, without forcing anything. So here's the turn. For the yogis in the dialogue, the breath was a thing to conquer. In this reading, the breath becomes a carrier, and what it carries matters more than how long you can hold it. Nothing here asks anyone to give up a breathing exercise. The Guru's point, as tradition reads it, is that the breath was never the goal. The Name inside it was.
screen: `THE YOGIS TRAINED THE BREATH.` · `NANAK ASKS WHAT IT CARRIES.` · `SAAS SAAS: WITH EVERY BREATH.` · `SIMRAN RIDES THE ORDINARY BREATH.` · then, large: `THE NAME IN THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simran on ten breaths. Sit, and don't change your breathing at all. Just let it come. If you're Sikh, or want to try it, let Waheguru ride each breath: wahe on the way in, guru on the way out. If you'd rather not, use a word that matters to you, or simply count. Ten breaths. If you lose count, start again without scolding yourself. When the ten are done, keep sitting, and notice that the breath keeps going without you. The bell holds the time.
The breath and the Name. In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis train the breath; Nanak points to what it carries. Guru Arjan's phrase: remember with every breath. Today's word.
screen: `THE BREATH AND THE NAME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the name in the breath. Today, at three ordinary moments, a door, a sink, a screen, take one breath on purpose and let something good ride it. Day one thousand one hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, and some match it to the breath, silently or aloud; the Sukhmani, with its call to remember with every breath, is recited in homes and gurdwaras.

match.prompt: what's inside the breath and the Name — tap the pairs.
pairs: points to what the breath carries

myth: in the Sidh Gosht, Nanak mocks the yogis' breath practice
he answers them and moves the center: the Word steadies a person, not the technique.
Guru Arjan's phrase is about every breath, not one long held breath
saas saas: remember with every breath, ordinary ones included.
simran means forcing the breath into a pattern
simran is remembering; some Sikhs let the Name ride the breath without forcing it.

fork.setup: the yogis raise their discipline of the breath. you're Nanak. what do you say?
options: that what matters is the Name the breath carries.
that he can hold his breath longer than they can.
fork.reveal: he answers without mocking, and turns the question: the Word inside steadies a person, not mastery of the breath.

original.note: remembrance: keeping the Name in mind, often by repeating it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lesson in breathing technique.
what it means: Nanak's answers point past technique to what the breath carries; the Name is the point.
what a scholar hears: the Sukhmani's saas saas simrahu Gobind makes remembrance as constant and ordinary as breathing.

sources.ref: Sukhmani, Gauri Mahala 5 ('saas saas simrahu Gobind')

notes: The Sidh Gosht's treatment of breath is summarized generally (the yogis' discipline includes breath work; Nanak's answers place the Word, not technique, at the center). Please confirm this is a fair reading and, if wanted, point to the specific stanzas on pavan (breath) to cite.

Sukhmani line 'saas saas simrahu Gobind' paraphrased as 'remember the Lord with every breath, and the worry inside the mind lifts'. Please confirm wording and add the Ang (believed to be around Ang 295).
Practice suggests 'wahe' on the in-breath and 'guru' on the out-breath; this is one common way, not the only one. Please confirm it is acceptable to present.
Practice and carry are invitations; a non-Sikh may use any word or simply count.

Editor: removed 'ashes' from the yogis' list (not checked in the Sidh Gosht; replaced with the patched coat, met on day 1136); removed the 'in paraphrase' framing and the claim that Nanak 'asks what the breath is carrying', since no single stanza says that, and recast it as a reading of his answers; replaced the general claim 'Sikhs don't ask anyone to give up their breathing exercises'. Possible stanza to cite: pauri 44, 'pavan arambh', where the answer names the breath as the beginning.
